title: Vetala Extended Tale 27: The Weaver and the Golden Loom

full_text:
Under the pale glow of the sickle moon, King Vikramaditya hauled the Vetala back across the eerie burning grounds. The Vetala whispered, "Hearken, O Vikram, to the riddle of the golden loom.

In Kanchipuram lived a master weaver named Padmakara. After seven years of solitary toil, he wove a garment of such dazzling beauty that it shimmered like distilled sunlight. The moment it was revealed, rival ministers of the court began scheming to seize it, and two wealthy merchants drew daggers in the marketplace to claim purchase rights. Bloodshed threatened the tranquility of the entire city.

Seeing the deadly envy his masterpiece awakened, Padmakara quietly tossed the magnificent fabric into the sacred fire before the king could claim it. The king was outraged at the destruction of unparalleled art and threw the weaver into prison. The townsfolk were divided: some called Padmakara a righteous peacemaker who snuffed out war; others condemned him as a vandal who destroyed a sublime cultural treasure out of arrogance.

Now, King Vikram," challenged the Vetala, "was Padmakara's act virtuous wisdom or haughty folly? Answer, or your crown will crumble along with your skull!"

King Vikram answered without hesitation: "Padmakara acted with supreme wisdom and compassion. The ultimate purpose of all art is to elevate the human spirit and bring joy to life. When an object—no matter how rare—becomes an altar for jealousy, greed, and murder, preserving human peace is infinitely superior to preserving silk and gold. His sacrifice showed detachment, not arrogance."

"Splendid judgment!" crowed the Vetala, and with a swift gust of wind, he flew back into the branches of the dark tree.
moral: Art that inflames strife and vanity ceases to be a blessing; true mastery seeks harmony above acclaim.
